entities.summary:
The 1998 United States embassy bombings were a series of coordinated terrorist attacks that targeted American embassies in Kenya and Tanzania on August 7, 1998. These bombings, carried out by al-Qaeda, resulted in the deaths of over 200 people and injured thousands more. The attacks were a major escalation of the global terror campaign led by Osama bin Laden and marked a significant turning point in the history of international terrorism.

The bombings occurred during the presidency of Bill Clinton, who was under pressure to respond to the attacks. The US launched a series of cruise missile strikes against al-Qaeda targets in Sudan and Afghanistan, but the strikes were largely symbolic and did little to address the root causes of the terrorism. The bombings also had a significant impact on the politics of the region, with the US increasing its military presence in East Africa and pressing for greater cooperation from African governments.

In the aftermath of the bombings, the US government imposed new security measures at its embassies around the world, including the use of metal detectors and explosive-detection equipment. The bombings also led to a significant increase in international cooperation against terrorism, with the US and other countries sharing intelligence and coordinating their efforts to combat al-Qaeda.

The 1998 embassy bombings will be remembered as a turning point in the history of international terrorism, marking a shift from small-scale attacks to large-scale, coordinated operations that targeted multiple locations simultaneously.
